div.p: In recent years, multiple data copies become popular in heterogeneous computing architectures. They enable parallel data transfer among diverse processing units. Tasks executed on such heterogeneous architectures often exhibit heightened resource competitions and intricate task dependencies, posing challenges in meeting strict timing constraints. Due to the dominant roles of data copies in the heterogeneous architecture, effective scheduling and tight response time analysis could contribute to the timing performance of the entire heterogeneous computing system. In this work, we introduce MATCH, which offers realtime scheduling and end-to-end response time analysis for the multiple parallel data copies that are popular in mainstream heterogeneous architectures. We first identify the aggravated resource competition and task dependency from multiple data copies and comprehensive task execution patterns. Then, we provide a real-time scheduling strategy and cross-granularity schedulability analysis to deal with resource competition and task dependency. Extensive evaluation demonstrates that efficient scheduling and analysis on multiple parallel data copies can significantly improve the schedulability by 55.5%-144.4%. Additionally, experiments conducted on various scales of heterogeneous systems demonstrate that MATCH can significantly reduce pessimism in response time analysis by up to 22.8%-57.5%. Importantly, the proposed approach is compatible with existing scheduling approaches that do not consider multiple parallel data copies and are readily applied to off-the-shelf heterogeneous computing systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Modern computing architectures designed for embedded or cloud-based applications are embracing heterogeneous architectures [1], [2] to meet the computational demands of sophisticated artificial intelligence (AI) applications [3]. These architectures seamlessly integrate multiple CPU cores with many parallel processing elements (PEs), such as GPU streaming multiprocessors (SMs) and FPGA IP cores, improving performance and energy efficiency. Notably, within these heterogeneous architectures, the transfer of data (i.e., copying) between CPUs and PEs can consume a significant portion of the end-to-end execution time [4], [5]. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the data transfer operations take a substantial portion, ranging from 7.8% to 59.9% in the general matrix multiplication (GEMM) and real-world applications on CPU-GPU § An Zou is the corresponding author. computing platforms [6]- [9]. These frequent and unignorable data movements between the CPU and PEs further make the memory movements the Achilles' heel in achieving strict timing constraints [10].

The data movements between the CPU and PEs are facilitated by the data copy engines (CEs) (as shown in Fig. 2), which are also known as memory copy engines in NVIDIA and AMD architectures. The CEs leverage the Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe), the Network on Chips (NoC), or other buses to enable swift and efficient data transfer. In recent years, processor vendors have been incorporating more CEs into heterogeneous architectures to support multiple and parallel data copies between CPU and PEs. For instance, in the GPUs detailed in Fig. 2, the number of CEs has increased from 1 to 8. However, the introduction of multiple and parallel data copy, especially in the presence of multiple CPU and PE cores, aggravates the complexity of the system, leading to two significant consequences [11], [12]. One is the unpredictable response time, and the other is low resource utilization due to the significant pessimism in scheduling analyses.

The improvements in real-time performance on heterogeneous architectures begin by enhancing the flexibility of PEs, often by supporting preemption and partitioning functionalities [13], [14]. Building upon this foundation, researchers have proposed various scheduling and response time analysis techniques, such as treating PEs as CPUs, incorporating selfsuspension [12], [15], employing the priority ceiling protocol [11], and developing heuristic approaches [16]. However, these The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II introduces the background and related works. Sec. III presents the modeling and task scheduling strategies on the heterogeneous architectures with multiple parallel data copies. Sec. IV provides the worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis and schedulability test for the entire system. Sec. V presents the parameter selection and summarizes the end-to-end scheduling. Sec. VI reports the experimental evaluations and Sec. VII and VIII conclude related work and this paper.

div.head: A. Heterogeneous Architectures
div.p: Heterogeneous computing architectures, which consist of CPUs and parallel processing elements (PEs), are gaining popularity in both embedded computing, such as the NVIDIA Jetson series, and high-performance computing, such as Oak Ridge's Titan supercomputer. These systems can improve performance at lower energy costs than homogeneous systems. Typically, when an application runs on a heterogeneous system, the CPU (host) handles I/O and serial computation while parallel executions are offloaded to the PEs (device). Data copy engines (CEs) manage offloading data to the PEs (hostto-device) and returning results to the CPU cores (device-tohost). Today's mainstream heterogeneous architecture features multiple CPU cores, several CEs, and many PEs. Tasks on this architecture are executed in an interleaved manner by the CPU cores, CEs, and PEs. A task can only use one of the CPU cores or CEs but can use many PEs simultaneously [17]. The CPU cores support preemptive execution, while the CEs and PEs are usually operating in a non-preemptive manner, and meanwhile, with the asynchronous operation mechanisms, the CPU calculation, data copies, and GPU kernels among different tasks can be executed in parallel [18]. Both the preemption [19], [20] and partitioning [21]- [23] of PEs (i.e., GPU and FPGA) are the meaningful research and engineering directions.

div.head: III. SCHEDULING STRATEGY AND SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: A. System Model 1) Hardware Features: Given a general heterogeneous architecture with N CP U CPU cores, N P E processing elements (PEs), and multiple data copy engines (CEs). These data copy engines includes N HE host-to-device data copy engines (HEs) and N DE device-to-host engines (DEs) [25], [26]. The task on the heterogeneous architecture incorporates the workloads that will be executed on these parts.

For the off-the-shelf heterogeneous computing system, the CPU cores are mostly with either x86 or ARM architecture, where a preemptive execution manner is generally supported in the CPU cores. As CPU segment takes charge of the I/O and control functions with rare parallel executions, every serial CPU segment only takes one CPU core to run, even if more CPU cores are available.

The clusters of PEs, such as GPUs [27], TPUs [28] and other machine learning accelerators [29], are incorporated by many parallel PEs. Given N P E PEs dedicated to a segment of length P which can be parallelized, the execution time follows the Amdahl and Gustafson's law [30],
div.formula: Execution Time " P 1 ´p `pNP E , (4
div.p: where p is the proportion of the PE segment that can be executed in parallel, and 1 ´p is the proportion that remains serial.

The data is transferred between CPU and PE memories via either a peripheral component interconnect express (PCIe) or a network-on-chip (NoC). Both PCIe and NoC offers multiple channels of packet-based data copies between any two endpoints. Each channel is driven by one data copy engine (DE or HE). It's worth noting that data copy through PCIe/NoC is non-preemptive once it starts [25].

2) Tasks on Hardware: A set of n independent parallel real-time tasks τ " tτ 0 , τ 1 , ..., τ n´1 u are executed on the heterogeneous architecture. The i `1-th task τ i comprises M i CPU segments separated by M i ´1 PE segments, with data copies between each CPU and PE segment. As the CPU is the central control unit in the heterogeneous architecture, the task starts and ends with a CPU segment. The task τ i has its deadline D i and release period T i . A segment is eligible to execute only after the completion of its previous segment. Therefore, task τ i can be characterized by a 3-tuple,
div.formula: τi " `pC 0 i , HD 0 i , P 0 i , DH 0 i , C 1 i , . . . , DH M i ´2 i , C M i ´1 i q, Ti, Di ˘,(5)
div.p: where C j i denotes the length of the j `1-th CPU segment, P j i the length of the j `1-th PE segment, HD j i the j `1-th data movement from CPU to PEs (host-to-device), DH j i the j `1-th data movement from PEs to CPU (device-to-host) in task τ i . Fig. 3 visualizes the task model and hardware features.

The task parameters, such as C j i , P j i , HD j i and DH j i for every segment, can be profiled ahead of scheduling with the measured worst-case execution time (WCET) in the above models. Since the proposed approach works on scheduling at the architecture level (i.e., cores and data copy engines), microarchitecture level variations like cache misses and benefits from data locality and placements are incorporated into the measurement of WCET. Notably, the proposed scheduling in MATCH is compatible with input from both measured runtime and the analytical runtime [31], [32].
The task execution on the heterogeneous architecture presents an aggravated hardware resource competition and application task dependency.
Hardware Resource Competition:

‚ In Spatial: The workload segments in the task should be executed on the corresponding processor, e.g. CPU segment should be on the CPU. ‚ In Temporal: The segment in the task only becomes available if the previous segment of that task is completed, e.g. the data copy happens after a CPU segment.

div.head: B. Scheduling Strategy
div.p: As described above, given the existence of multiple CPU cores, several HEs, DEs, and many PEs, during the scheduling and response time analysis, we need to deal with the competition and dependencies from different tasks simultaneously. Therefore, we propose a fixed-priority-based scheduling strategy, considering its applicability to the general heterogeneous architectures, which exhibits the following execution patterns.

‚ CPU segments: are executed on the CPU cores scheduled by the real-time scheduler in the operating system with fixed priority. ‚ PE segments: are executed on the PEs. The PEs are partitioned into n groups, and group i has a fixed amount of PEs dedicated to the i-th task. ‚ Data Copies: are executed on the HE or the DE. The data copy from the host to the device will be released immediately when its previous CPU segment is finished, inheriting the priority of its previous CPU segment. The same applies to the data copied from the device to the host. Unlike the CPU segment, the data copy works in a non-preemptive manner.

To guarantee that the proposed scheduling strategy can meet the timing requirement, we provide a detailed response time analysis and schedulability test methods in Sec. IV. The task priorities, and the spatial partitioning on the PE, serve as two searching parameters that are determined in Sec. V. During the runtime, the proposed scheduling strategy leverages the support of the operating system without introducing any system-level overhead.

div.head: IV. RESPONSE TIME / SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: To capture the competition and dependencies aggravated by the multiple and parallel data copies, cross-granularity analyses are presented from spatial and temporal dimensions. Fig. 4 visualizes the top-down overview of the analysis procedure, with spatial dimension (Finer Spatial Partition Granularity) on the top and temporal dimension (Broader Temporal Analysis Scale) at the bottom. First Task & Processor Partitioning decomposes the problem recursively, targeting finer spatial granularity. In each partitioned group, a series of analyses with a broader temporal scale is performed: Single-Segment Analysis bounds the response time for every individual segment; Multiple-Segment Analysis adopts a wider temporal scope and bounds the response time for several consecutive segments; Task-Level Analysis is the largest possible granularity and bounds the response time for each task.

div.head: A. Task and Processor Partitioning
div.p: Given the heterogeneous architecture with multiple data copy engines, we can conduct a response time analysis and perform a schedulability test on the entire system. If the system fails the schedulability test, we can partition the tasks and cores into smaller groups and repeat the response time analysis until we identify a schedulable configuration. The recursive partitioning strategy operates as follows:

‚ Perform a completed analysis pipeline for full hardware resources. If the schedulability test passes, we assert the system is schedulable and exit the analysis procedure. ‚ If not, the hardware resources are partitioned and the tasksets are separated into each group. The system is guaranteed to be schedulable only if each partition passes the schedulability test. ‚ If any partition does not meet the timing requirement, we proceed to check its second-level partition and so on. The procedure will continue until the current partition does not include any multi-core architecture or all the sub-partitions in the same layer pass the test. As an intuitive example, Fig. 4 partitioned the CPUs to 2+2, HEs(DEs) to 1+1, PEs to 6+3, and tasksets to 3+2. Suppose that "HW Partition 2" passes the schedulability test while "HW Partition 1" does not, the first partition further breaks to "Partition 1.1" and "Partition 1.2" to conduct the analysis.
Generally speaking, Eq (6) describes a hardware resources partition scheme with g groups:

div.head: B. Single-Segment Analysis
div.p: This section aims to find the worst-case response time (WCRT) for the data copy segment. We will focus on host-todevice (HTD) copies, as the analysis methods are analogous to device-to-host (DTH) copy segments. We start from the base case that N HE " 1 (Theorem IV.2), and then scale to multiple HEs or DEs (Theorem IV.3). The main notations appear in the analysis in shown in Tab. I.

Based on the fixed-priority scheduling strategy and nonpreemptive task execution pattern, we anatomize the response time of a copy segment HD j i into three parts: 1. Blocking time due to a (partial of) lower priority task segments, 2. Waiting time for higher priority task segments, 3. Execution time (aka length) of the segment itself.
Theorem IV.1 Given the j `1-th HTD data copy segment of task τ i , its response time HR j i can be expressed as
div.formula: HR j i " HB j i `HA j i `HD j i ´1,(7)
div.p: where HB j i is the length of blocking, HA j i is the time waiting for higher priority tasks until the segment has been executed for at least 1 unit.

PROOF. In the above equation, HD j i is the segment length, within which the first unit is executed at the end of HA j i . Since the data copy segment is non-preemptive, once it gets scheduled, its executing time always equals the segment length. Therefore the response time equals the summation of the above three elements.

In the above theorem, HD j i is a fixed value and we are seeking the worst-case value of HR j i . Therefore, we can boil down the question of finding WCRT into 1 finding the upper bound of the blocking HB j i (denoted as z HB j i in the following) and 2 finding the upper bound of HA j i (denoted as z HA j i ). In the following texts, we stick to this backbone and provide an optimized solution to the two questions. div.head: C. Multiple-Segment Analysis
div.p: While the single-segment analysis provides an assuring upper bound for each segment's response time, this approach exhibits significant pessimism:

‚ For question 1 , we may overestimate the blocking time due to lower priority tasks. When analyzing the response time of every segment, we always take the longest segment as the blocking upper bound z HB j i . This pessimism increases when the task to analyze possesses relatively high priority and there is a few extremely long segments, which leads to a lengthy blocking in the analysis. ‚ For question 2 , we leverage the workload function in a shortsighted manner. To evaluate z HA j i , we always consider the worst-case interference that can happen since the release of HD j i , while the actual workload is lighter from a wider scope. Mathematically speaking, the workload function satisfies the property W k pt 1 q `Wk pt 2 q ě W k pt 1 `t2 q, and the equality is less likely to happen when the time interval enlarges. This pessimism increases when the task possesses relatively low priority, which aggravates workload accumulation. The two drawbacks mentioned above will scale with the number of tasks and number of processors, bringing significant analysis pessimism for systems with multiple processors and large tasksets. Hence, it becomes essential to address these two issues for the complex system we are modeling, based on which the following subsection provides a tighter bound of response time.

div.head: V. PARAMETER SELECTION AND SCHEDULING
div.p: This section presents the offline searching and runtime scheduling of the proposed MATCH framework. For the offline searching, we leverage the schedulability test in Sec. IV-E as a checking tool; while for the runtime scheduling, we adhere to the scheduling strategy outlined in Sec. III-B.

During the offline searching phase, we determine the optimal task priority assignments and partitioning of processing elements (PEs) for each task. The end-to-end schedulability test is used in each search iteration to validate the chosen priorities and partitioning. Once a feasible scheduling solution is identified, the relevant parameters are recorded, and we proceed to the runtime scheduling phase. The OS's kernel real-time scheduler (SCHED FIFO) automatically schedules tasks based on the assigned priorities and PE partitions. The detailed process is shown in Algo. 2.

MATCH is an offline timing analysis framework that provides timing guarantees before deployment. For future works, a possible extension is to first find all feasible priority assignments by MATCH offline, which are then stored in a list. During runtime, the scheduler can dynamically adjust priorities, if the new priority assignment is in the precomputed list. However, more analytical efforts have to be made to ensure safety during the transition process.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, extensive experiments are performed to evaluate the response time analysis and scheduling performance of MATCH with both numerical simulation and GEMM Break out of all for loops; 6 // Runtime scheduling: 7 Set priorities and PE partitioning by the searched result; 8 Launch and schedule tasks using the operating system. and AI workloads on real heterogeneous computing architectures equipped with multiple copy engines (HEs and DEs).

div.head: A. Response Time Analysis of MATCH
div.p: We first focus on the response time analysis performance of our proposed method. We examine MATCH under different configurations (i.e., numbers of): executor property, taskset property, and segment property.

1) Task Generation: To present the schedulability of the proposed approach under different configurations, we measured the acceptance ratio with respect to targeted utilization. The acceptance ratio is the number of schedulable tasksets divided by the number of tasksets. For fair comparisons, we apply similar methods in existing works [12], [15], [24], [35] to generate the CPU, data copy, and PE segment lengths, where we randomly generate all segment lengths, uniformly distributed within the range of [1,10]. The deadline D i of task i is set according to the generated segment lengths and its utilization rate:

div.p: The default heterogeneous computing platform has 2 CPU cores, 2 parallel data copies (1 HE and 1 DE), and 10 PEs, with 10 parallel tasks run on this platform. A detailed summary of task generation is presented in Table II.

2) Schedulability under Different Configurations: Executor Number: We first investigate the impact of the number of CPU cores and engines on the schedulability. The results are presented in Figs. 6a and6b, respectively. As either the number of CPU cores or the number of data copies increases, the acceptance ratio of MATCH improves; however, the number of data copies has a more pronounced effect on schedulability than the number of CPU cores. When compared to the case with only 2 engines, the acceptance ratio increases significantly with one more engine in either direction. If equipped with 4 engines (2 HEs+2 DEs), we can partition the taskset into 2 groups, each containing 5 tasks with 1 HE + 1 DE, leveraging the recursive partition scheme of MATCH to achieve a doubled performance 1 . On the other side, the improvement diminishes when the number of CPUs exceeds three, indicating that data copies become a bottleneck when the number of CPUs is greater than three.

Taskset Property: Next, we evaluate the impact of the number of tasks and task utilization variation, as shown in Fig. 6c and Fig. 6d. As the number of tasks increases, the schedulability gradually decreases and stabilizes when the number of tasks reaches 12 or more. This is because the analytical pessimism caused by task interactions worsens as the task count increases. We also examine the performance when the utilization of each task varies. In each experiment, the maximum utilization difference between any two tasks in the task set is constrained to the interval [20pi ´1q%, 20i%], where i " 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Fig. 6d shows that MATCH achieves comparable scheduling performance even as utilization varies.

Segment Property: The results in Fig. 6e show that with more segments in a task, the overall schedulability decreases. The observed declines in response time can be attributed to the growing interaction and competition among tasks, which exacerbate the pessimistic impact on response time. We evaluate MATCH with different segment scaling between CPU, data copy and PE segments. For instance, in the legend of Fig. 6f,1:1:5 represents the PE segment length varies from [1,50], while CPU and data copy segments follow the default configuration. According to our experimental results, 5:5:5 reaches the same schedulability as 1:1:1, meaning that MATCH performs well despite different segment lengths.

div.head: B.
div.p: Comparing MATCH with SOTA 1) Scheduling Approaches: We compare the following state-of-the-art scheduling algorithms, which support end-toend real-time scheduling and response time analysis. 1) Self-Suspension (SS) [24]: the pseudopolynomial-time analysis, where we transform every task into a nonsuspending task by modeling every suspension interval (processing element (PE) and data copies) as computation segments. 2) SHAPE [35]: real-time scheduling for multiple CPU cores and many PEs with superior schedulability on general heterogeneous architectures. 3) RTGPU [34]: scheduling for self-suspension model under fixed priorities. This approach achieves good schedulability on a single CPU, one data copy (shared by two directions), and many PEs configurations. 4) STGM [12]: real-time GPU scheduling of hard deadline parallel tasks on partitioned PEs with great schedulability. Busy-waiting scheduling and self-suspension scheduling are designed and analyzed. We first focus on architectures with one CPU and multiple copy engines, including configurations with one CPU, one HE, and one DE (1+1+1), one CPU with three engines (1+2+1), and one CPU with four engines (1+2+2). As shown in Fig. 7, when the number of parallel copies increases, MATCH significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. On a 1+1+1 platform, MATCH achieves a maximum schedulable utilization of 0.75, compared to 0.45 for the best-competing method, yielding a 55.5% improvement. Remarkably, for a platform with one CPU and two engines in both directions, MATCH delivers a substantial 144.4% improvement. This performance gain is due to MATCH's efficient use of all engines in both directions, which enhances response time analysis on single-CPU heterogeneous architectures, whereas other methods typically use only one engine.

When multiple CPUs are present in the computing platform, other algorithms are typically optimized for n `n `n configurations, where tasks are divided into n groups of 1+1+1 configurations, with data copies shared in both directions. Adding an additional CPU nearly doubles the performance of these approaches, as it allows the activation of an extra engine. Hence, MATCH achieves better schedulability than state-of-the-art methods because it can incorporate a third data copy, and isolate the HTD and DTH copy during the analysis. Since all the approaches follow fixed-priority and static partition scheduling, we search for the optimal task priority and PE partitioning. During the runtime, we implement the persistent threads [27], [36] to support the partitioning of PEs (i.e., Streaming Multiprocessors in GPUs).

2) Schedulability Under GEMM Workloads: Following the previous schedulability analysis, each task in a taskset is randomly generated with the configuration in Table II. The synthetic tasks perform 32-bit floating-point (FP32) general matrix multiplication (GEMM) determined by the segment length. The deadlines are set to the same values as the periods. Using these three real heterogeneous computing architectures with different numbers of data copies, we examine the schedulability across different CPU and data copies under different scheduling approaches. Fig. 9a, 9b and 9c illustrate the acceptance ratios achieved by different approaches and real systems. Compared with various schedulability approaches, MATCH demonstrates its primary strength in scheduling computing platforms of any size, encompassing different numbers of CPU cores and parallel copies in either direction. Notably, MATCH outperforms other scheduling methods in computing platforms involving 2 HEs + 2 DEs, benefiting from the partitioning strategy. The performance has a similar trend to that of GEMM workloads, where MATCH performs better than other approaches, especially on the uni-core system. It reduces the pessimism (measured by distance from the maximum schedulable utilization of the real system) by 22.8-57.5% compared to the best of other methods. The schedulability in all the scheduling approaches and the real system is not increased significantly after the N CP U goes over 2. This is because, in the fully connected neural network, the memory copy is dominant and becomes a bottleneck, taking 51.8% of the total execution time, while the CPU segments are shorter.

To assess the scalability of the proposed MATCH method, we conducted schedulability evaluations with varying network layers, ranging from the default 6 layers to 18 layers, as illustrated in Fig. 11. As the number of network layers increases, all response time analysis methods, as well as the real system scheduler, exhibit degraded performance due to the increased complexity of the task structure. Nevertheless, MATCH consistently outperforms other methods and demonstrates the closest alignment with the schedulable utilization of the real system.

div.head: Evaluation Conclusion
div.p: The proposed scheduling and response time analysis method effectively captures the temporal behavior in off-the-shelf heterogeneous systems with multiple and parallel data copies, as validated by both synthetic and AI workloads. Furthermore, MATCH is designed to be broadly applicable to general heterogeneous computing systems, including GPUs, FPGAs, and DSPs.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORK
div.p: General heterogeneous computing platforms contain CPU cores, data copies, and PEs. The research of real-time scheduling related to heterogeneous computing architectures starts from the flexibility of the PEs. Researchers treat the heterogeneous PEs as a non-preemptive entity [37]. Further, to overcome the limitation of blocking from lower priority tasks, many works extend the PEs with the preemption function [38], [39]. For example, Park et al. [40], Basaran et al. [41], Tanasic et al. [42], and Zhou et al. [13] propose architecture extensions to improve the preemption and tested on the processor simulators. Alongside preemption, partitioning is another direction most of the processor vendors currently choose to support the flexibility of PEs with low design costs [43]. For example, Multi-Process Service (MPS) and Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) have been introduced by NVIDIA to support multiple task concurrency with assigned numbers of PEs to each task [44]. AMD also released open-source software support for hardware partitioning [23]. After improving the flexibility of PEs, researchers began to optimize the endto-end scheduling. Huang et al. [24] present a scheduling algorithm and response time analysis for single-core CPUbased heterogeneous architectures. Zou et al. [34] develop a scheduling mechanism for single CPU-based heterogeneous systems with the fine-grained utilization of PEs. Xu et al. [35] introduce a scheduling algorithm and response time analysis for multi-core CPU-based heterogeneous architectures. Saha et al. [12] introduce a software-hardware solution for efficient spatial-temporal scheduling for GPU. Alongside the workload function, Patel et al. [11] extend the existing Multiprocessor Priority Ceiling Protocol (MPCP) schedulability analysis for the heterogeneous architecture. Although multiple parallel data copies have become commonplace in modern heterogeneous architectures, state-of-the-art approaches often overlook the benefits of these copies. This work introduces a real-time scheduling strategy and response time analysis specifically designed to optimize the scheduling of multiple data copies within heterogeneous computing architectures.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: To effectively schedule the tasks on today's heterogeneous architecture equipped with multiple and parallel data copies, we present MATCH -a real-time scheduling method encompassing scheduling and detailed response time analyses, accompanied by schedulability tests. MATCH offers a crossgranularity scheduling solution in both spatial and temporal dimensions for the multiple and parallel data copies, efficiently coordinating various resources while maintaining compatibility with other scheduling algorithms. We conducted empirical evaluations of our approach using both schedulability analysis and GEMM and AI workloads, involving real embedded, desktop, and server heterogeneous computing systems. The results demonstrate significant schedulability enhancements can be achieved by effectively scheduling multiple and parallel data copies.
